items.passage:
Ten-minute grocery delivery looks like a miracle of logistics, and in one sense it is. A customer taps a phone, and a rider arrives with milk, bread and eggs before the kettle has boiled. Behind that tap sits a dense network of small dark stores, each stocked with the few hundred items that sell fastest in one neighbourhood, plus software that predicts demand street by street and hour by hour. The model works only because the stores are close: a rider travelling two kilometres can make the trip in ten minutes, while a rider travelling eight cannot. That simple fact of distance explains the whole economics of quick commerce. 
The costs are what make the model fragile. A dark store pays city rent for space that earns nothing from walk-in customers, and it must stock enough variety to satisfy orders while throwing away what does not sell before it expires. Riders are paid per order, so their earnings depend on a steady flow of orders that rain, festivals and rival offers can interrupt without warning. The companies themselves have spent heavily on discounts to win customers, betting that habit, once formed, would survive higher prices. When one company raised its delivery fee, a visible share of its customers moved to a rival within a week, and when the rival raised its fee in turn, some customers simply went back to the neighbourhood shop. Loyalty, it turns out, is mostly a function of price.
The neighbourhood shop, meanwhile, has not stood still. Many kirana stores now take orders on messaging apps and deliver within the hour, using family labour and stock they already hold. They cannot match ten minutes, but they offer credit to known customers, they know which brand of tea a household prefers, and they do not charge a delivery fee. The quick-commerce companies argue that their advantage is selection and reliability: the app shows exactly what is in stock, the price is fixed, and the delivery time is promised. Wealthier, time-pressed households use the app; price-sensitive households and those who value credit stay with the shop.
Regulators have begun to ask questions that the early growth phase postponed. The first is about rider welfare: if a rider is paid per order and the platform controls the assignment of orders, is the rider genuinely independent, or is the piece rate simply a wage with the risk shifted onto the worker? The second is about competition: when a platform sells its own private-label goods alongside the brands it lists, does it favour its own products in search results? 
The likely future is a compromise that neither side will celebrate. Quick commerce will survive, but in fewer cities and with higher fees, serving customers who genuinely value speed over price. Kirana stores will survive too, absorbing the delivery habits they learned during the quick-commerce boom. Riders will probably gain some protections, such as accident cover and a minimum per-order payment, paid for by slightly higher prices. The ten-minute promise will remain, but only where the density of orders justifies it, and the industry's early claim that it would replace the neighbourhood shop will quietly be forgotten. What will remain is a useful, narrower service: fast delivery for a few things, in a few places, for people willing to pay for it. That is a smaller ambition than the one investors funded, but it is a real one, and it may be the only one the economics can support.

items.passage:
Every large company now publishes a sustainability report, and nearly every report claims progress. Emissions are falling, water use is down, and the supply chain is being cleaned up. The trouble is that the claims are hard to check, and the incentives to exaggerate are strong. Investors increasingly direct money toward funds labelled green, customers say they prefer sustainable brands, and regulators in several countries have begun to require disclosure. A company that reports honestly about slow progress risks losing investment to a rival that reports glowing progress, whether or not the rival's numbers are real. This is the engine of greenwashing: not usually an outright lie, but a careful selection of what to measure, what to leave out, and how to frame the result.
The techniques are well documented. One is to report intensity rather than totals: emissions per unit of output can fall while total emissions rise, if output grows faster than efficiency improves. A second is to choose a convenient baseline year, such as a year when emissions were unusually high, so that the fall since then looks dramatic. A third is to buy carbon offsets and report the net figure prominently, while the gross emissions that the offsets supposedly cancel continue to grow. A fourth is to define the boundary narrowly, counting the emissions of the company's own offices and factories but excluding the suppliers and customers who account for most of the total. Each technique is defensible in isolation, which is what makes the practice hard to police: a company can always argue that it followed the reporting standard, even when the standard leaves the important choices to the reporter.
The damage is not only to the climate. When exaggerated claims crowd out honest ones, investors cannot tell which companies are genuinely improving, so capital flows to the best storytellers rather than the best performers. Consumers who pay a premium for a green product and later learn that the claim was hollow become cynical, and their cynicism then punishes honest companies too. Regulators face a different problem: every new rule creates a new boundary to game, and the firms with the largest compliance teams are often the best at gaming it. 
There are remedies, and they are becoming clearer. The first is standardisation: one set of reporting rules, with fixed boundaries and fixed baseline years, so that companies cannot shop for the version that flatters them. The second is assurance: independent audits of sustainability data, with the same seriousness as financial audits, including penalties for misstatement. The third is to report totals alongside intensities, gross figures alongside net ones, so that a reader can see both the efficiency gain and the absolute change. But together they change the calculation: a company that must publish audited totals under fixed rules has far less room to select its way to a good story.
The deeper lesson is about what disclosure can and cannot do. Disclosure can make dishonesty harder and more expensive, but it cannot make a company sustainable. A firm can report its emissions perfectly and still be in a business whose core product is incompatible with a low-carbon future. Investors and regulators who focus only on the quality of the reporting risk mistaking a well-reported problem for a solved one. The real question is not whether a company's sustainability report is accurate, but whether its business can survive in a world that actually limits emissions. That question no report can answer, and it is the one that matters most.

For a student chosen among the 36 cricket players, the probability of playing all three games is t/36, so its least possible value is 8/36 = 2/9. The bound is attainable: 10 play cricket only, 13 football only, 9 hockey only, 9 play cricket and football only, 2 play football and hockey only, 9 play cricket and hockey only, and 8 play all three. That gives 36 cricket, 32 football and 28 hockey players, exactly 20 playing exactly two games, and 60 students in all. items.explanation: Let the number who do all three be x. Then exactly two is 2x, and at least two is 2x + x = 3x = 36, so x = 12 and exactly two is 24. Everyone is accounted for by only-one (30 + 25 + 20 = 75), exactly-two (24), all-three (12) and none, so none = 150 - 75 - 24 - 12 = 39. Using the exactly-two count, or the all-three count, or adding the all-three count to the answer, gives the other options.
